result: Listeners demonstrate high sensitivity to detecting coherent figure patterns emerging from random background tones in the SFG stimulus (Experiments 1-2). Performance depends on coherence (number of repeating components) and duration, with hit rates reaching 93±2% for the most salient conditions. Listeners can identify specific figures as distinct perceptual objects in an AXB discrimination task.
status_reasoning: Reviewers explicitly affirm these findings, stating 'subjects are able to "hear out" a sequence of tones embedded in a complex acoustic environment' and 'most subjects are able to segregate the foreground sound pattern (one sound source) from the background sound source.' They note 'studies were appropriately performed with adequate controls.'

result: Figure detection performance scales with the number of repeating chords rather than their absolute duration (Experiment 3). Performance with 25 ms chords showed no significant difference from 50 ms chords, suggesting temporal scaling of the segregation mechanism.
status_reasoning: While reviewers do not explicitly critique this finding, they express disappointment that 'the motivation for each modification of stimulus parameters should be explained more clearly' and ask 'What would their model predict for the manipulation?' This suggests uncertainty about the interpretation and theoretical grounding of this manipulation.

result: Listeners maintain above-chance performance when figure components follow frequency ramps rather than fixed frequencies (Experiment 4). Performance decreases with steeper ramps (ramp=5 vs ramp=2), suggesting greater susceptibility to spectral than temporal perturbations.
status_reasoning: Reviewers specifically request model predictions for this manipulation, stating 'it is unclear why the model simulations are not shown for all experimental manipulations' and 'it would be nice to see what the model predicts for the ramped SFG.' This indicates the reviewers find the interpretation incomplete without modeling support.

result: Removing background-only chords that precede the figure does not affect detection performance (Experiment 5), suggesting segregation is not mediated by adaptation to ongoing background statistics.
status_reasoning: Reviewers request clearer motivation for stimulus manipulations, asking 'What would their model predict for the manipulation?' The lack of model predictions for this condition leaves the mechanistic interpretation uncertain despite the behavioral finding.

result: Figure detection remains robust when noise bursts are interleaved between chords (Experiment 6). Listeners show above-chance performance even with 500 ms noise interruptions, demonstrating integration over remarkably long time windows (up to 3 seconds total).
status_reasoning: Reviewers explicitly highlight this finding as remarkable, stating 'it is remarkable that segregation of the foreground tone sequence still occurs despite introduction of interleaved bursts of white noise between the foreground tones. The duration of the white noise could extend up to 500 ms.' They affirm these findings without critique.

result: The long temporal integration windows (up to 500 ms) implicate cortical mechanisms at or beyond primary auditory cortex, as such long windows have rarely been reported in auditory object formation.
status_reasoning: Reviewers explicitly agree with this interpretation, stating 'These findings are clearly beyond the segregation capacities of core auditory cortex and the authors rightfully suggest non-classical auditory cortical processing stations as being the most likely generators of this percept.'

result: The behavioral results cannot be explained by standard adaptation-based models from the streaming paradigm. Figure and background overlap in frequency space, challenging segregation based on spatially distinct A1 populations. Performance depends on the number of simultaneously repeating components, suggesting integration across widely spaced frequency channels.
status_reasoning: Reviewers implicitly accept this claim by affirming the need for alternative models and explicitly stating the temporal coherence model is 'the most appropriate model for explaining how this foreground/background segregation develops,' which presupposes inadequacy of adaptation-based models.

result: The psychophysical data are consistent with a temporal coherence model of auditory segregation. Model simulations show similar profiles to behavioral results for coherence and duration manipulations, constituting the first demonstration of temporal coherence model compatibility with complex acoustic scenes.
status_reasoning: While reviewers state 'the authors concisely provide modeling data and evidence that the temporal coherence model is the most appropriate model,' they express disappointment with 'the integration between data and modeling' and note 'it is unclear why the model simulations are not shown for all experimental manipulations, but only for number of tones and frequency components.' This incomplete modeling coverage creates uncertainty about the full support for temporal coherence.

result: Previous fMRI work found no A1 modulation during passive listening but strong IPS activation modulated by figure salience. IPS may represent a neural correlate of the figure percept, with representation depending on temporal coherence computation across frequencies initially represented in auditory cortex.
